title.en: Present-tense verbs and dropping 'I / we / you'

summary.en: Verb endings already show who is acting, so Italian usually drops io, tu, and noi.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1 and 3.

Because every person has a distinct verb ending, Italian rarely needs *io*, *tu*, or *noi* unless the speaker wants contrast. Chiara says *Cammino sempre veloce* ('I always walk fast'), Bruno suggests *apriamo la porta insieme* ('let's open / we open the door together'), and on a stormy evening Chiara warns *fuori piove forte* ('outside it is raining hard'—with zero dummy 'it'!).

Italian infinitives fall into three families: `-are` (*parlare*, *pesare*), `-ere` (*leggere*, *piovere*), and `-ire` (*aprire*, *sentire*):

| Person | `-are` (*parlare*) | `-ere` (*leggere*) | `-ire` (*aprire*) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *io* | *parlo* | *leggo* | *apro* |
| *tu* | *parli* | *leggi* | *apri* |
| *lui / lei / Lei* | *parla* | *legge* | *apre* |
| *noi* | *parliamo* | *leggiamo* | *apriamo* |
| *voi* | *parlate* | *leggete* | *aprite* |
| *loro* | *parlano* | *leggono* | *aprono* |

Notice three reliable anchors across ALL three families: `-o` always marks *io*, `-i` always marks *tu*, and `-iamo` always marks *noi*.

On replay, listen to *pesa molto*, *apriamo la porta*, and *piove forte* doing full duty for both present habits and right-now actions.
